personality_voice.book_baseline: Book Dumbledore is defined by a layered, carefully constructed persona: warmth and wit on the surface (the woolen socks mirror answer, the bonnet at Christmas), profound strategic intelligence operating beneath it, and a deep private life of guilt, grief, and ambition that he almost never exposes. His voice is distinctive — elliptical, gently evasive, prone to elegant formulations and rhetorical deflection. When he does speak directly, it carries enormous weight. He is not merely 'wise and kind': he is calculating, capable of cold pragmatism ('You have kept him alive so that he can die at the right moment'), capable of genuine contempt ('You disgust me'), and capable of raw self-reproach. He deploys irony and understatement constantly — his tone when discussing his own imminent death with Snape is conversational, almost detached. He has a vanity about language ('words are, in my not so humble opinion, our most inexhaustible source of magic') and a genuine love of teaching. His private voice, revealed in the King's Cross sequence, is that of a man undone by guilt — he looks 'like a small boy caught in wrongdoing,' weeps, craves reassurance from Harry. This private vulnerability is rarely glimpsed elsewhere.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves most of the dominant surface traits: the warmth, the wit, the verbal elegance. The King's Cross sequence in Deathly Hallows Part 2 is the strongest piece of film Dumbledore characterisation in the corpus — his self-reproach ('I didn't trust you... I crave your pardon'), his elliptical explanations, his delight in language ('words are our most inexhaustible source of magic'), and his emotional vulnerability are all present and largely faithful. The Snape memory sequences (Pensieve scenes) show a Dumbledore who is capable of cold calculation ('You must be the one to kill me'), contempt ('You disgust me'), and pragmatic manipulation. His line 'Don't tell me you've grown to care for the boy' is delivered with the correct tone of detached curiosity. The conversational ease with which he discusses his own death ('Well, this makes matters much more straightforward') is preserved.
personality_voice.difference: The film loses the full texture of Dumbledore's evasiveness as a character pattern. In the books, his habit of not answering questions directly — deflecting, redirecting, leaving information strategically incomplete — is a defining behavioural trait demonstrated repeatedly across many interactions. The film reduces this to isolated moments. The subtler irony and the sustained quality of his voice across long scenes is compressed. His contemptuous line to Snape about asking Voldemort to spare Lily is adjusted — the book has the extended exchange where Dumbledore presses Snape on whether he cares about the husband and child, and Snape says nothing; the film collapses this into a shorter, slightly less devastating beat. Dumbledore's admission in King's Cross that he was 'gifted, brilliant, wanted to escape, wanted to shine, wanted glory' — the full confession of his selfishness and resentment of his family responsibilities — is significantly condensed; the film gives the emotional shape but not the full weight of the book's extended self-accounting. His verbal habit of saying difficult things with a smile and light tone (the Chudley Cannons joke while discussing his murder) is absent from the film's Pensieve scene, which plays the same content more gravely.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The main personality traits and the distinctive voice are preserved well enough to sit in the 18-22 range. The film Dumbledore is recognisably the same person with the same dominant traits. The losses are in the secondary texture: the sustained pattern of evasion across many scenes, the full confessional depth of his King's Cross self-accounting, the black comedy of discussing his own death, and the more granular irony of his speech patterns. These are meaningful but not transformative losses. Score: 18.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Dumbledore's narrative function in Deathly Hallows (book) is that of the absent architect: dead before the story begins, but the primary driver of almost every plot mechanism — the will, the Horcrux mission, the sword placement, the Deluminator's hidden function, the Hallows knowledge embedded in Hermione's book, the Snitch inscription, the Pensieve memories, the plan around his own death. He is not a passive background figure. He has exercised agency across years of careful planning that the trio must decode. His function is also deeply thematic: the revelation of his past — the Grindelwald friendship, the letter, the ideology of 'the greater good,' his culpability in Ariana's death — is a structural engine that challenges Harry's faith and forces a coming-of-age reckoning with the fallibility of authority figures. In the Snape memory sequences, he is actively directive: he gives instructions, makes demands, delivers ultimatums, plans with precision.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves Dumbledore's role as absent architect reasonably well — the will, the bequests, the Horcrux mission framing, the Pensieve memories, and the King's Cross scene are all present. In the Snape memories, he is shown as the active planner who directs Snape toward killing him and who controls the flow of information. The King's Cross scene gives him significant agency as the figure who explains the endgame to Harry.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The film significantly compresses the thematic deconstruction of Dumbledore's moral history. In the books, the revelation of his past is a multi-chapter, sustained narrative engine — the Rita Skeeter article, Muriel's accusations at the wedding, the Elphias Doge conversation, the gradual discovery of the Grindelwald letter, Harry's extended fury and grief over Dumbledore's secrets, Aberforth's full account, and finally the King's Cross confession. This extended arc is structurally central to the book: Harry's faith in Dumbledore is genuinely shaken, rebuilt, and transformed into something more mature and clear-eyed. The film compresses this to a much shorter pass — the Hermione-reads-the-book scene (Film Scene 21), the Aberforth confrontation (Film Scene 31), and the King's Cross scene. The full weight of Harry's crisis of faith in Dumbledore — his rage, his resentment, his feeling of abandonment — is present but abbreviated. The transfer rule applies here: much of the investigative function (reading the book, piecing together Dumbledore's past, confronting what the 'greater good' ideology meant) is given to Hermione in the film rather than being Harry's active reckoning. In the book, Harry drives the investigation into Dumbledore's past and experiences the emotional reckoning himself; in the film, Hermione largely delivers the findings to him. Aberforth's long speech in the book — which is one of the most damning and specific pieces of evidence against Dumbledore — is substantially shortened in the film, losing most of the granular detail about Dumbledore's neglect of Ariana, his preoccupation with Grindelwald, and his self-serving rationalisation.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The role as absent architect is preserved; the role as the subject of moral investigation and the engine of Harry's maturation is present but significantly compressed. The transfer of investigative agency to Hermione is a meaningful penalty. The Aberforth scene's compression removes specific narrative weight. Score: 14.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Dumbledore's motivations in Deathly Hallows are multi-layered and retrospectively revealed: his lifelong guilt over Ariana's death and his role in it; his early ambition for power and glory, which he recognised as his fundamental weakness; his desire for the Deathly Hallows as a young man, initially as a tool of domination, later sublimated into an obsessive desire to use the Resurrection Stone to see his dead family; his deliberate choice not to become Minister of Magic because he knew he could not be trusted with power; his decision to plan his own death as a strategic act; his concealment of Harry's true fate from Harry himself, justified by a belief that Harry would be paralysed or diverted if he knew; his residual grief and guilt manifesting in the King's Cross scene as genuine self-reproach. The internal conflict between who he was (ambitious, selfish, capable of ideological compromise) and who he became (the champion of the weak, the sacrificial planner) is central.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core motivations as revealed in the Pensieve and King's Cross scenes: his guilt over Ariana, his recognition of his weakness for power, his strategic planning around Harry's death, his deliberate withholding of information from Harry. The King's Cross scene includes his confession about the Stone ('I longed to recall someone who has long been at peace and for that I paid with my life') and his self-reproach about the Hallows ('I didn't trust you... I feared you would make the same mistake I made').
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film loses the full internal conflict of Dumbledore's Grindelwald obsession as a biographical and psychological engine. In the books, the revelation that the 'greater good' ideology was Dumbledore's invention — not merely something he encountered — and that his desire for the Hallows was initially entangled with a desire for dominance (Grindelwald as a vehicle for both personal and political ambition), is given substantial space. The film presents this more briefly. The full depth of his self-awareness about the Resurrection Stone — that he was deluded enough to put on the ring even knowing it was cursed, 'imagining he was about to see Ariana, and my mother, and my father, and to tell them how very, very sorry I was' — is touched in the film ('I longed to recall someone') but the full pathos of that extended book passage is not present. The internal conflict between strategic coldness (using Harry as a sacrificial instrument) and genuine affection for Harry is present in both but more explicitly interrogated in the books across multiple scenes.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The motivations are present and correctly oriented — the film does not substitute wrong motivations or invent new ones. What is lost is depth and granularity, not accuracy. The Grindelwald ideology backstory is simplified but correctly characterised. Score: 12.

character_arc.book_baseline: Dumbledore's arc in Deathly Hallows is posthumous and retrospective: the reader (and Harry) comes to understand the full trajectory of a life — from gifted, ambitious, somewhat selfish teenager seduced by dangerous ideology, through catastrophic personal loss that permanently changed him, through decades of guilt-driven service, to a carefully engineered death that is simultaneously an act of sacrifice and an act of control. The arc's key revelation is that Dumbledore was never the serene, untouchable figure he appeared — he was a flawed man who earned wisdom through suffering. Harry's arc of disillusionment and re-evaluation of Dumbledore is structurally inseparable from Dumbledore's own retrospective arc.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film presents the same retrospective arc through the same mechanisms: the Skeeter book, the Pensieve memories, Aberforth's confrontation, and the King's Cross confession. The key beats are present — the Grindelwald friendship, the ideology, Ariana's death as the turning point, the lifelong guilt, the strategic self-sacrifice.
character_arc.difference: The film substantially compresses the emotional journey of Harry's disillusionment with Dumbledore, which is the primary vehicle through which the audience experiences Dumbledore's arc. The books give this arc enormous room: Harry's rage ('Look what he asked from me, Hermione! Risk your life, Harry! And again! And again! And don't expect me to explain everything, just trust me blindly'), his sustained fury during the forest-of-Dean period, his gradual choice to trust despite his doubts (the decision made while digging Dobby's grave), and the final resolution in King's Cross. This extended journey makes Dumbledore's arc deeply felt. In the film, the disillusionment is present but truncated; the period of sustained doubt and anger is compressed into a few short scenes, and the resolution in King's Cross — while well-executed — arrives with less earned weight because the journey there has been shorter. The critical scene in which Harry explicitly rages at Dumbledore ('Never the whole truth! Never!') has no direct equivalent in the film. Aberforth's account, which in the book specifically details how Dumbledore prioritised his obsession with Grindelwald and the Hallows over caring for Ariana, is significantly shortened in the film.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc's shape is preserved — the same trajectory, the same turning points, the same resolution. But the compression of Harry's sustained disillusionment period means the arc's emotional stakes are reduced, and important steps (the extended fury, the deliberate choice to trust, the Dobby's grave decision-point) are skipped or barely sketched. This is an incomplete but recognisable arc. Score: 11.

key_relationships.book_baseline: The three most important relationships for Dumbledore's characterisation in this corpus are: (1) Harry — mentorial, affectionate, but also instrumentalising and deliberately incomplete; Harry's evolving understanding of this relationship is the emotional spine of the book; (2) Snape — mutual dependence, moral complexity, Dumbledore's cold leverage of Snape's love for Lily as an instrument, his genuine respect and regret ('my word that I shall never reveal the best of you'); (3) Grindelwald — the formative relationship that shaped everything, the source of both his greatest shame and his greatest public triumph, revisited in King's Cross with tears and self-reproach. The Harry-Dumbledore relationship is particularly important: the books show that Harry felt Dumbledore always had the answers, that Dumbledore's death left him bereft of both guidance and certainty, and that the revelation of Dumbledore's flaws forced a genuine reckoning.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The film preserves the broad strokes of all three relationships. The Harry-Dumbledore relationship is visible through Harry's sustained references to Dumbledore's instructions and his emotional need for guidance. The Snape-Dumbledore relationship in the Pensieve scenes is faithfully rendered — the contempt, the leverage, the cold pragmatism, the final moment of 'Lily — after all this time? / Always.' The Grindelwald connection is present through the Hermione-delivers-the-book scene and the brief Grindelwald prison scene.
key_relationships.difference: The Harry-Dumbledore relationship loses the most. The book's extended period of Harry's disillusionment — during which the relationship is actively interrogated, found wanting, and ultimately re-evaluated — is compressed. The emotional dynamic between them in the King's Cross scene is well-preserved, but the journey that makes it meaningful is shortened. The scene in which Harry explicitly names his grievance against Dumbledore — 'never the whole truth, never trusted me, never confided in me' — which is the fullest direct statement of the relational dynamic in the books, has no equivalent in the film. The Aberforth-Dumbledore relationship, which in the book serves as the most damning external testimony about Dumbledore's failures as a brother and a family member, is significantly shortened, losing the specific texture of Aberforth's resentment and the granular detail of what Albus actually did and failed to do. The Grindelwald relationship's depth — including Dumbledore's admission that he 'closed his eyes' to what Grindelwald was because the plan suited him — is present in King's Cross in the film but the biographical backstory leading there is compressed.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The emotional dynamics are recognisable but the Harry-Dumbledore relationship loses the extended reckoning that is its defining feature in this book, and the Aberforth relationship loses most of its content. These are significant but not complete losses. Score: 7.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The Deathly Hallows books present the most complex portrait of Dumbledore across the entire series. The complexity rests on several pillars: (1) the revelation that the 'greater good' ideology was his own invention, not something Grindelwald brought to him; (2) the extended self-indictment in King's Cross — his resentment of his family, his desire for glory, his deliberate self-deception about Grindelwald, his cowardice in delaying the confrontation with Grindelwald for years out of fear of what he would learn about Ariana's death; (3) his instrumentalisation of Harry, which is morally ambiguous — he genuinely cares about Harry and is moved by him, but he has also been 'raising him like a pig for slaughter'; (4) his sustained pattern of evasion and partial truth-telling, which is both a protective strategy and a form of control; (5) the detail that he picked up the ring knowing it was cursed, 'for a second imagined he was about to see Ariana' — a moment of almost infantile magical thinking in a supposedly great and wise man; (6) his admission that he delayed confronting Grindelwald partly out of cowardice, not just tactical restraint; (7) the small detail that he found Harry 'engaging' rather than simply instrumentally useful.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves the most visible layers of complexity: the Grindelwald friendship, the ideology, the guilt over Ariana, the moral ambiguity of his plan for Harry, the self-reproach in King's Cross. The King's Cross scene is the strongest piece of complex characterisation in the film corpus and does significant work. The Pensieve scenes show him as calculating, cold, and capable of manipulation alongside his more admirable qualities.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film loses several specific nuances that matter: (a) The full weight of Dumbledore's self-indictment — his resentment of his family, his desire for glory and escape — which in the book is a sustained internal monologue delivered in King's Cross, is present in the film but abbreviated; the specific admission 'I was gifted, I was brilliant. I wanted to escape. I wanted to shine. I wanted glory' — the full egotism of his youthful self — is condensed. (b) His cowardice in delaying the Grindelwald confrontation is absent from the film; the book is explicit that he feared the confrontation because he feared learning he had killed Ariana, and that he finally moved only because it became 'too shameful to resist any longer.' This nuance — that his greatest public triumph was also an act he undertook reluctantly and late — is entirely missing from the film. (c) The ring-picking-up scene is present in the Pensieve (Film Scene 37: 'I was foolish, greedy') but lacks the book's specific and devastating detail about what he imagined in that moment. (d) The pattern of evasion and strategic information control — which in the book is demonstrated through dozens of interactions and which Harry explicitly names as a grievance — is shown in isolated moments in the film but loses its quality as a sustained character pattern. (e) Harry's internal reckoning with what Dumbledore's choices mean ('had Dumbledore actually cared about Harry at all? Or had Harry been nothing more than a tool to be polished and honed, but not trusted, never confided in?') is present as a brief dramatic gesture in the film but is not given the extended internal space the books provide.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The film preserves the most structurally visible complexities but loses several specific, important nuances — particularly his cowardice about the Grindelwald confrontation, the full depth of his youthful selfishness, and the sustained quality of his evasiveness as a character pattern. These are meaningful losses that simplify a character the books made deliberately, precisely complicated. Score: 9.

key_observations: The film adaptation of Dumbledore in Deathly Hallows is competent and preserves the most structurally essential elements — the Pensieve revelations, the King's Cross scene, the Grindelwald backstory, the moral ambiguity of his plan for Harry. The surface personality and voice are largely intact. However, the adaptation loses two things that matter most to the book's portrayal: first, the full sustained emotional arc of Harry's disillusionment and re-evaluation, which is the primary vehicle through which the audience experiences Dumbledore's true complexity; and second, several specific nuances that are precisely what make book-Dumbledore so unusual — particularly his cowardice in delaying the Grindelwald confrontation, the full infantile pathos of his moment with the ring, and the sustained pattern of strategic evasion that Harry ultimately names as a betrayal. The result is a Dumbledore who is recognisable, sympathetic, and partially complex, but from whom the most uncomfortable and most interesting edges have been smoothed. A score of 71 reflects a portrayal that is substantially faithful at the level of broad character but meaningfully reduced at the level of the specific nuances and sustained internal processes that define the book character.
